 MVPete: PCA’s Incredible Season
 Rohan Theis , Staff Writer 
 • 
 October 31, 2026 
 Minda Haas Kuhlmann Pete Crow-Armstrong takes an at-bat while playing for the Tennessee Smokies. (CC BY 2.0) 
 “M-V-P! M-V-P!”
 Wrigley Field, home of the Chicago Cubs, has been erupting with chants in support of Pete Crow-Armstrong’s strong case to win the National League MVP award. His spectacular offense and league-leading defense have made him the heavy favorite to win the award, well ahead of the two-year-in-a-row reigning winner, Shohei Ohtani.
 How did this happen? What did PCA change to insert himself into this conversation?
 First off, Fielding Run Value (FRV) is an advanced statistic that estimates the number of runs a player saves a team because of their defense. Essentially, the higher a player’s FRV, the more valuable they’ve been for their team. Pete Crow-Armstrong leads the league with a +27 FRV. That means that he saved a tremendous total of 27 runs for the Chicago Cubs in 2026, solely through his defense.
 His defense is aided by his incredible athletic ability. PCA has a 29.5 ft/s sprint speed, a league-leading jump, and a catch-making ability that allows him to make catches quite literally never made before. 
 “He’s just so fast and athletic,” sophomore Teo Schlater said. “He makes so many plays. … PCA’s so fun to watch in center field.”
 Additionally, PCA’s defense has always been a part of his game. What’s really shocked the Cubs and the league this season has been the huge jump in his hitting. At the end of the 2026 regular season, he ended up tied for the most home runs with 45, the most runs at 112, the most extra-base hits, and the most total bases in all of Major League Baseball.
 PCA is also the seventh player in Major League history to hit 40 home runs and have 40 stolen bases in one season. In franchise history, he’s the 13th Cub to hit for the cycle, and the first Cub ever to hit for back-to-back 30/30 seasons.
 Still, despite his success and recognition from his coach, his season did not start the way many fans expected it to.
 “[The start of PCA’s season] was really disappointing,” sophomore Nico Meno said. “He played really well last season, and he was supposed to be a centerpiece of the team.”
 Something had to change. He settled on an adjustment that moved his feet drastically closer in the batter's box, as well as moving his hands below his chest as opposed to shoulder height. After the adjustment, his average jumped by nearly 100 points, and his on-base plus slugging increased by nearly .500.
 He’s also dramatically improved his plate discipline, taking more balls and drawing more walks. A year ago, he was bottom 10 in the league in walk rate and on-base percentage. This year, he’s number seven.
 “He’s definitely [walking] noticeably more,” Teo said. “I feel like it’s a sign of maturity and growth.”
 His stellar case for MVP has improved his odds to win from +1000 in late May and June (or a 1 in 10 implied probability) to -20000 (basically guaranteed). Moreover, Ohtani’s persistent knee injuries have increased these odds, barring the two-time MVP from pitching at all in the second half of the season. Ohtani’s recurring injuries, as a result, have sparked debate about whether PCA is truly the most valuable player.
 “Even if [Shohei] was healthy, I think PCA would still have a good shot at winning the MVP,” Nico said.
 Whether or not you think PCA deserves the [National League] MVP award, his fans will never lose hope. Nico said. “He’s one of the best, if not the best, baseball player in the league.”
